title: Why hasn't Rama come?
hook: Sita asks two hard questions out loud, and neither one is scolded
carry: the avatar's promise: when dharma falls, he comes

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sita called Hanuman's news nectar mixed with poison. Your line: viraha, the ache of missing is love too.
screen: `VIRAHA: THE ACHE OF MISSING IS LOVE TOO.`

segments.voice: People sometimes imagine Sita as endlessly patient, never questioning, never afraid. Valmiki's Sita is braver than that: she doubts out loud. A woman who has been tricked once, terribly, by someone in disguise, doesn't trust easily. A woman who has waited this long for rescue is allowed to ask why it hasn't come. Valmiki gives her both doubts, and doesn't scold her for either.
screen: `NOT ENDLESSLY PATIENT.` → `SHE DOUBTS OUT LOUD.` → `TWO DOUBTS, NO SCOLDING.`

segments.voice: The first doubt comes the moment Hanuman climbs down toward her. Sita shrinks back. What if this is Ravana again, in a new disguise, the way he once came to her hut dressed as a holy man? She says it to his face. Then she checks her own heart: when I look at you, my mind is glad. Would it be glad if you were Ravana? So she asks to hear about Rama, and she listens. The second doubt comes after the ring, and it's sharper. If Rama loves me, why hasn't he come? He and Lakshmana are mighty archers. It's the question of everyone who has waited for help that's slow, and Valmiki lets her ask it. Hanuman doesn't scold her. He answers: Rama doesn't know where you are. The moment I tell him, he'll come. For Hindus, that answer reaches far past Lanka. Rama is honored as an avatar of Vishnu, God come down into the world. And in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna, another avatar, makes the promise himself: whenever dharma declines and wrong rises, I come, age after age, to protect the good. So Hindus can ask Sita's question out loud, why haven't you come yet, and it isn't a failure of faith. Sita asked it. The answer she got wasn't a rebuke. It was: he's on his way.
screen: `WHAT IF YOU'RE RAVANA AGAIN?` · `WHY HASN'T RAMA COME?` · `HE DIDN'T KNOW WHERE YOU WERE.` · then, large: `WHEN DHARMA FALLS, HE COMES.`

segments.voice: If you pray, bring the thing you're waiting on to God plainly, the way Sita asked: why not yet? Then rest for a few breaths in the Gita's promise: whenever dharma falls, I come. If you don't pray, name what you're waiting for honestly, without pretending you're not tired of waiting, and let each out-breath be a little more patient than the last.
Her doubt. Sita's fear that Hanuman is Ravana in disguise, and her question of why Rama hasn't come: two doubts, honestly asked, and answered without a rebuke.
Your line: the avatar's promise, when dharma falls, he comes. Tomorrow, a rescue offered on the spot. Day six hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Some readers point to Sita's questions to Hanuman as signs of her strength, and many Hindus recite the Gita's 'yada yada hi dharmasya' verse as God's promise to come when dharma declines.
